Paper Content:
Summarization Metrics for Spanish and Basque
Summarization Metrics for Spanish and Basque:
Do Automatic Scores and LLM-Judges Correlate with Humans?
Jeremy Barnes∗
jeremy.barnes@ehu.eus
Naiara Perez
naiara.perez@ehu.eus
HiTZ Center
University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU)
Alba Bonet-Jover
alba.bonet@ua.es
Department of Software and Computing Systems
University of Alicante, Spain
Begoña Altuna
begona.altuna@ueu.eus
GOI Institute, Basque Summer University (UEU)
Abstract
Studies on evaluation metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge models for automatic text summarization have largely been focused on English, limiting our understanding of their effectiveness
in other languages. Through our new dataset BASSE (BAsque and Spanish Summarization
Evaluation), we address this situation by collecting human judgments on 2,040 abstractive
summaries in Basque and Spanish, generated either manually or by five LLMs with four
different prompts. For each summary, annotators evaluated five criteria on a 5-point Likert
scale: coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance, and 5W1H. We use these data to reevaluate
traditional automatic metrics used for evaluating summaries, as well as several LLM-asa-Judge models that show strong performance on this task in English. Our results show
that currently proprietary judge LLMs have the highest correlation with human judgments,
followed by criteria-specific automatic metrics, while open-sourced judge LLMs perform
poorly. We release BASSE1 and our code publicly, along with the first large-scale Basque
summarization dataset containing 22,525 news articles with their subheads.
1. Introduction
Automatic text summarization seeks to create a concise and fluent text that captures the
main ideas from one or more documents (Giarelis et al., 2023). This task has been studied in
depth in Natural Language Processing (NLP) (Dang, 2006; Dang & Owczarzak, 2008) and
plays an important role in mitigating excess information in an age of increasing information
glut (Navas-Martin et al., 2012).
Although extractive approaches, where sentences and phrases are taken directly from
the original document, were originally more common (McDonald, 2007; Lin & Bilmes,
2011), current approaches instead generally rely on abstractive methods, where the model
generates novel sentences to capture the most salient information. This change in modeling
paradigm also leads to new challenges for evaluation, as abstractive models are more prone
to hallucinating information (Maynez et al., 2020; Vasilyev et al., 2020; Laban et al., 2022).
∗. All authors contributed equally.
1. The dataset is available under open licenses at https://github.com/hitz-zentroa/summarization.

Barnes, Perez, Bonet-Jover, & Altuna
In order to evaluate automatic summaries, researchers generally rely on three main
strategies: i) human evaluation, ii) evaluation using reference summaries and automatic
metrics, and iii) evaluation via Large Language Models (LLMs), often referred to as LLMas-a-Judge. Human evaluation over a small number of important criteria, e.g., coherence or
fluency, is often chosen to give high-quality evaluation of abstractive summaries. However,
this approach is slow, expensive, and does not lend itself to internal evaluations while iterating
over models. Therefore, most research instead relies on automatic metrics, e.g., ROUGE
(Lin, 2004) and, more recently, LLM-as-a-Judge (Leiter et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Lyu
et al., 2025).
Selecting appropriate metrics or judge LLMs relies on meta-evaluations (Bhandari et al.,
2020; Fabbri et al., 2021; Deutsch et al., 2022) that measure the correlation between human
evaluations and automatic evaluation methods. While these studies provide invaluable information, they have only been performed comprehensively for English, leaving the assessment
of their performance in other languages to be explored.
We therefore address this gap by collecting human annotations for automatic summaries
in Basque and Spanish—languages with respective fragmentary and medium coverage of
language resources (Giagkou et al., 2023). Specifically, we collect abstractive summaries
generated by five LLMs and four different prompts on 45 news articles in each language.
We then collect human judgments for each summary with respect to five criteria—namely,
coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance, and 5W1H. With this novel dataset, BAsque and
Spanish Summarization Evaluation (BASSE), we then proceed to address the following
research questions:
RQ1: Do automatic metrics for evaluating summarization correlate well with human
judgments in Basque and Spanish?
RQ2: Do judge LLMs have the ability to replicate human judgments for summarization?
RQ3: Which summary criteria (coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance, and 5W1H )
do state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with in Basque and Spanish?
Our results indicate that proprietary LLM-as-a-Judge models currently have the highest
correlation with human judgments on our data, while several traditional metrics also correlate
well with specific criteria. On the contrary, open-source judge LLMs currently do not correlate
well with human judgments on our data. Our contributions are hence the following:
• We present a new multilingual corpus (Basque, Spanish) of summaries generated by
five LLMs manually annotated for five criteria on a 5-point Likert-scale;
• We study the correlation between human judgments with the results of automatic
evaluation metrics and LLM judges in languages other than English;
• We additionally provide the first corpus for summarization in Basque, consisting of
22,525 news articles and their subheads.

Summarization Metrics for Spanish and Basque
2. Related Work
Two main approaches exist in summarization: extractive and abstractive (El-Kassas et al.,
2021). The extractive approach selects and takes the most relevant sentences directly from
the input document, concatenating them to create the summary. On the other hand, the
abstractive approach generates a set of novel sentences to represent the main information of
the original document, rather than copying directly from the original text. In the case of
automatic summarization, abstractive summaries are “more similar to those produced by
humans” (Giarelis et al., 2023) and have become more popular as summarization models
have improved.
English datasets for training and evaluating summarization models range from the original
Document Understanding Conference (DUC) and Text Analysis Conference (TAC) shared
tasks (Dang, 2006; Dang & Owczarzak, 2008), which are relatively small but high quality, to
automatically collected datasets, such as CNN/DailyMail (Hermann et al., 2015) or XSUM
(Narayan et al., 2018), which rely on collecting news articles paired with their subhead as a
proxy for a human-generated summary.
Non-English languages have fewer resources available and most use news articles paired
with their subhead (Scialom et al., 2020; Varab & Schluter, 2021). There are notable
exceptions that instead collect human-generated summaries (Segarra Soriano et al., 2022;
Gonzalez-Agirre et al., 2024), but for most languages there are no high-quality resources
available for evaluating automatic summaries.
2.1 Manual Evaluation
Manual evaluation of automatic summaries has long been the gold standard approach, ranging
from direct annotation of criteria to the pyramid method (Nenkova & Passonneau, 2004).
This evaluation can be done through directly annotating each summary for certain criteria—
coherence of the generated text, relevance of the selected material, etc.—or alternatively by
ranking automatic summaries with respect to one of these criteria. In addition, as abstractive
summaries have become more common, evaluating their consistency (factuality/faithfulness)
has become increasingly important as well (Maynez et al., 2020; Vasilyev et al., 2020; Laban
et al., 2022).
Importantly, crowdsourcing often leads to poor results when evaluating automatic summarization (Gillick & Liu, 2010; Hardy et al., 2019; Fabbri et al., 2021) and expert evaluation
can also fail to achieve good levels of inter-annotator agreement (Steen & Markert, 2021;
Iskender et al., 2021). This can be mitigated to a degree by setting up well-defined annotation
guidelines in order to achieve reliable human evaluation

This evaluation can be done through directly annotating each summary for certain criteria—
coherence of the generated text, relevance of the selected material, etc.—or alternatively by
ranking automatic summaries with respect to one of these criteria. In addition, as abstractive

has become increasingly important as well (Maynez et al., 2020; Vasilyev et al., 2020; Laban
et al., 2022).
Importantly, crowdsourcing often leads to poor results when evaluating automatic summarization (Gillick & Liu, 2010; Hardy et al., 2019; Fabbri et al., 2021) and expert evaluation
can also fail to achieve good levels of inter-annotator agreement (Steen & Markert, 2021;
Iskender et al., 2021). This can be mitigated to a degree by setting up well-defined annotation
guidelines in order to achieve reliable human evaluation of text summarization.
2.2 Automatic Evaluation
Manual evaluation becomes an impossible task as corpus size increases, motivating the
need for automatic metrics for summarization evaluation. Reference-based metrics include
ROUGE (Lin, 2004) and its many variants (Rankel et al., 2013; Graham, 2015), which use
n-gram overlaps between reference and automatic summaries. S3 (Peyrard et al., 2017) is
instead a learned metric that combines the output of other metrics as features and learns
to predict human scores directly. Similarly, referenced-based Natural Language Generation

(NLG) evaluation metrics, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), BertScore (Zhang et al.,
2020), CHRF, or CIDEr, are also commonly used.
Reference-free metrics have also been proposed (Louis & Nenkova, 2009a, 2009b; Saggion
et al., 2010). SummaQA (Scialom et al., 2019), for example, automatically creates questions
from the source document and scores the summary depending on its ability to answer these
questions. BLANC (Vasilyev et al., 2020) instead measures how much a summary helps a
language model predict words from a sentence taken from the original document.
More recently, using LLMs to automatically evaluate summaries—LLM-as-a-Judge—has
shown promise (Leiter et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Lyu et al., 2025). These models often
show higher correlations with human judgments than previous token-based metrics.
However, nearly all of these metrics and models have been designed for English and their
ability to correctly evaluate non-English summaries has not been deeply studied. In this
line, Lloret et al. (2018) highlight the importance of not relying solely on summarization
evaluation metrics conceived for English texts. It is furthermore nontrivial to transfer many
of these metrics to new languages, as they require a number of resources to already exist.
2.3 Meta-evaluation of Automatic Metrics
Meta-evaluation of automatic metrics is necessary to establish the reliability of the metrics.
This is typically done by studying the correlation between metric scores and human judgments
(Lin, 2004).
Fabbri et al. (2021), for example, collect human evaluations for 23 English summarization
models over four dimensions: coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance. They then
calculate correlations between these annotations and automatic metrics and find that few
automatic metrics correlate well with the human annotations.
Despite some studies on Spanish and French (Saggion et al., 2010), there has been little
meta-evaluation done on other languages. Clark et al. (2023) create a multilingual summary
dataset with six languages and also collect binary yes/no crowd-sourced annotations for six
criteria, although interannotator agreement (IAA) is quite low, with Krippendorf’s α below
0.5 for 5 of 6 criteria. They then train a referenceless metric and compare it with ROUGE-L,
but do not perform a comprehensive study of evaluation metrics. Similarly, Aharoni et al.
(2023) create a multilingual summary dataset of 45 languages and crowd-source annotations
for two criteria. They then compare ROUGE-L and an NLI-based faithfulness metrics on
these data. Finally, Koto et al. (2021) meta-evaluate a number of automatic metrics on
summaries generated by BERT and pointer-network models in eight languages.
However, none of the meta-evaluations performed on non-English languages study a range
of automatic metrics and most of them use automatically extracted subhead-article pairs as
a proxy for reference summaries, which limits the reliability of the findings.
3. Methodology
We develop our multilingual summarization evaluation dataset through three main steps.
First, we collect news articles from quality sources in both target languages (Section 3.1).
Second, we generate a battery of summaries that includes original subheads, human-written
summaries, and automatic summaries from various LLMs using different prompt strategies
4

Summarization Metrics for Spanish and Basque
(Section 3.2). Finally, we conduct expert annotation using five criteria through a multi-round
process to ensure reliable assessments (Section 3.3).
3.1 Data Collection
Data collection has been conducted with the idea of exploiting some of the most representative
data available. We randomly collected news articles covering diverse topics and genres to
ensure variety across both languages.
For Basque, we collect 45 articles from Berria,2 the main newspaper in this language,
including metadata concerning the URL, date of publication, assigned topic category, title of
the article, subhead, as well as the body of the text.3 Berria offers its contents under CC
BY-SA 4.0 license.4
For Spanish, another set of 45 news articles was randomly extracted from the test set of
the MLSUM dataset (Scialom et al., 2020). The Spanish subset of MLSUM contains news
articles of El País newspaper5 and provides (news body, subhead, URL) triplets. MLSUM is
distributed under MIT license, complying with our needs for redistribution.
3.2 Summary Collection
For each of the 45 articles in both languages, we collected three types of summaries, the final
multilingual dataset comprising 90 source articles and 2,040 summaries:
Subhead: Following standard practice in news summarization literature (Hermann
et al., 2015; Narayan et al., 2018), we extracted the original subheads from each article
to serve as baseline summaries.
Human: We collected manually written summaries from our expert annotators. For the
first 15 articles, which were used to compute annotation agreement (as explained below
in Section 3.3.2), each of the three annotators produced a summary. The remaining 30
articles were divided among the annotators, yielding a total of 75 manual summaries
per language.
Automatic: We generated automatic summaries using five different LLMs, each
prompted in four different ways, resulting in 900 automatic summaries per language.
The specific models and prompting strategies are described in the following subsections.
This comprehensive approach to summary generation was designed to achieve high
variability in summary characteristics, thus providing a diverse dataset for evaluating
different metrics and LLMs.

3.2.1 Model Generation
We used five different LLMs: Microsoft Copilot (2024),6
Bart Machine (2023),7
Hugging Face (2023),8
BingoLing (2022),9
and 7B Generation (2023).10
Each model was provided with four different prompting strategies, leading to 20 automatic
summaries per model and language.11
The prompting strategies were:
1. Summarize the article in 100 words: This prompt asks the model to condense the
entire article into a concise summary.
2. Summarize the article focusing on the main points: This prompt instructs the model
to highlight the most important points of the article.
3. Summarize the article focusing on key facts: This prompt is similar to the second but
emphasizes facts over points.
4. Summarize the article using the subhead as a prompt: This approach asks the model
to take the subhead as the starting point and generate a summary that covers the main
points of the article, using the subhead as a prompt.
5. Summarize the article using the subhead and the body as a prompt: This is a more
intuitive approach where the model is given both the subhead and the body as context.

3.2.2 Evaluation of Automatic Summaries
Each automatic summary was evaluated for fluency, coherence, relevance, consistency, and
5W1H criteria.12
1. Fluency: This refers to the grammatical correctness and coherence of the generated text.
2. Coherence: This refers to the logical flow and coherence of the generated text.
3. Relevance: This refers to how relevant the generated text is to the original article.
4. Consistency: This refers to how consistent the generated text is with the original article.
5. 5W1H: This refers to the criteria of Who, What, Where, When, and How, which are standard
criteria for summarization evaluation.

5

Barnes, Perez, Bonet-Jover, & Altuna
3.3 Annotation Process
We developed a multi-round process to ensure high reliability and consistency in our annotations.
The process starts with three annotators for the first 15 articles (to compute annotation
agreement), and then assigns the remaining 30 articles to two annotators each, ensuring that
each annotator works on 15 articles. Each annotation round involves the following steps:

3.3.1 Initial Annotation
Each annotator reads the article and generates a manual summary. This summary is then
compared to the subhead and other automatic summaries. The annotator rates the summary
on the five criteria mentioned above, using a 5-point Likert scale.

3.3.2 Refinement Rounds
If the initial annotations show high inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorf’s α ≥ 0.8),
we proceed to the next step. Otherwise, we perform a refinement round where each annotator
reads the summary and provides feedback, leading to a reevaluation of the criteria.

3.3.3 Final Annotation
After multiple rounds of refinement, we ensure that all annotators have a consistent set of
annotations, with inter-annotator agreement (IAA) ≥ 0.8 for all criteria.

3.3.4 Ground Truth Annotation
We also created a set of ground truth annotations by having a panel of annotators manually
rate each summary based on predefined criteria. This step was done after the initial process to
ensure that all annotations are consistent and accurate.

4. Results
We present our findings in four main sections:
4.1 Human Evaluation: We evaluate the performance of the automatic metrics and judge
LLMs in terms of their correlation with human annotations.
4.2 LLM-as-a-Judge: We assess whether judge LLMs have the ability to replicate human
judgments for summarization.
4.3 Automatic Criteria: We analyze the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs across the
different criteria.
4.4 Correlation with Human Evaluations: We discuss the correlation between automatic
evaluation metrics and human evaluations across different languages.
